newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebel advances further splinter Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rebel advances further splinter Zaire.

text.p: As rebel advances in eastern Zaire prompt speculation about the imminent breakup of the vast, chaotic country, there is strong evidence that many regions have already gone their own way.

"It is no secret that Zaire only really exists on the map, which is not necessarily a bad thing. What we have to hope for is that the latest crisis doesn't spread and result in the destruction of all the constituent parts," said one Western diplomat in Kinshasa.
Zaire's people, disillusioned and impoverished by years of corrupt rule, seem united only by shared circumstances in which all face a battle to survive, despite the country's vast mineral wealth.

"Anything we do here we have to do for ourselves, the government is interested in nothing but taking money," says businessman Kalonje wa Tshimanga, part of a community trying to build its own hydroelectric dam in the central Kasai region.

Zaire already has a variety of national currencies. The Kasai only accept notes which went out of circulation everywhere else in 1993 -- and faith in new Zaire notes is so weak that the United States dollar is the de facto means of exchange.
Like Kasai, copper-rich Shaba also enjoys de facto autonomy.

Zaire has been further riven by the Rwandan-backed rebellion launched near the eastern frontier in October which has now spread deep into Zaire. Guerrilla fighters say they have attacked the town of Kindu, 320-km (200-miles) from the border.

For many of Zaire's over 40 million people the only contact with the state is with its nominal agents in the form of the military or the internal security service, which treats Zaireans as foreigners when they travel inside their own country.

The real strength of the security they provide was shown up by the rebels who routed the army within days, driving ragged, unpaid troops back to their nearest bases hundreds of kilometres (miles) from the fighting, raping and pillaging as they retreated.
The infrastructure of Zaire, Africa's second largest country, has crumbled, leaving isolated cities tenuously joined by pot-holed roads and dilapidated railways.
When the first trains got through to southeastern Zaire after a long break last year they found villages without soap, without matches, even without sugar and salt.

For 30 years President Mobutu Sese Seko has ruled Zaire by dividing enemies and allies alike. His people have been left to fend for themselves through a system of national corruption which did nothing to preserve the fabric of a modern society.
The president has been in Europe since August for cancer treatment, depriving his nation of its one symbol of national unity. There is no clear sign when he will return.

Mobutu came to power when Zaire was fragmenting through civil war following independence from Belgium in 1960. The self-proclaimed "Great Helmsman" always presented himself as the one man who could hold Zaire's more than 250 ethnic groups together.

Kasai and southern neighbour Shaba both do more trade with Johannesburg than Kinshasa and even before the rebel invasion eastern Zaire was more closely linked to Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda in trade terms than the capital.
And yet in every region there is the belief that somehow elections now scheduled for 1997, but appearing increasingly unlikely, will somehow save Zaire from itself and bring what everyone wants.

In Kinshasa the elections are expected to get rid of the president. In Kasai the elections are expected to bring veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi to power. In Shaba they will bring still more autonomy to a region that has on several occasions tried to secede.

"If elections are not held in the rest of Zaire by May we will hold our own and go our own way," says Lukonde Kyenge of the Union of Federalists and Independent Republicans, Shaba's most popular party.
